messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Moana Tui is a 46-year-old married forensic analyst who came to treatment more than a year after her younger brother died suddenly in a violent accident. She had been the family member asked to identify him. What stayed with her was not a full narrative of that day but a set of brutal fragments: the fluorescent hum in the viewing room, the sound of her own breath turning ragged, and the clipped voice of a staff member saying her brother’s name. In her mind, the memory returned as still pictures rather than a continuous sequence—the edge of the sheet, his hand, the unnatural color of his face. When it came back, she did not just see it; she sometimes heard the sounds from that room again, as if they had been preserved intact. The force of it was so immediate that she had to shut it down, turning away mid-thought or leaving the room because she felt flooded too quickly to bear it.

In the months after his death, Moana had come to believe that something fundamental had ended. She said her life had been destroyed by what happened, not in a dramatic sense but as a settled fact: the future she recognized was gone. She no longer felt any sustaining trust in people, in life, or in anything larger that might make suffering tolerable. Alongside that was a deadened conviction that nothing in her life meant much anymore. Those conclusions shaped how the memory sat inside her. Because she experienced the death as proof that life was empty and unsafe, the fragments of the viewing room came back with the force of that meaning attached to them, each snapshot feeling less like a past event than confirmation that everything had been permanently ruined. Even brief contact with the memory became overwhelming.

Her work made it hard to keep distance from anything associated with death. As a forensic analyst, she spent her days in labs and offices where case files, evidence logs, and matter-of-fact discussions about bodies were ordinary. She began avoiding work whenever she could, taking sick days, arriving late, and sometimes sitting in her car in the parking lot unable to make herself go in. The sterile lighting and clipped procedural language at work were close enough to the atmosphere of the identification room that she dreaded being pulled back into those frozen images and sounds. At home she started staying up very late, scrolling aimlessly or watching television until the early morning because sleep felt like surrendering control; in the quiet of bed, the pictures and the remembered voices came fastest. She also began restricting her eating, describing it less as hunger loss than as a way to keep herself tightly managed, numb, and contained.

These habits gradually tightened around her. By avoiding work and delaying sleep, Moana gave herself fewer chances to feel steady or competent, and the long nights left her more frayed, more vulnerable to the memory intruding without warning. Skipping meals added to the sense that she was running on fumes. When the snapshots returned, they seemed sharper, and the sounds in her head more vivid, at exactly the times she was most depleted. She would try to think about her brother and immediately hit that same wall of emotion, as though the memory could only arrive at full intensity. The more she organized her days around not going in, not sleeping, not eating, the less her life resembled the one she had before his death, and this seemed to prove to her that the trauma had in fact destroyed everything worth recognizing.

That conclusion fed the habits further. Because nothing felt meaningful anymore, work seemed pointless; because she had lost faith in life itself, caring for her body felt irrelevant; because she was certain her old life was gone, there seemed to be little reason to keep ordinary routines. Her husband had started pleading with her to eat dinner with him or come to bed before dawn, and she often withdrew from those conversations with a flat certainty that he could not understand what had been broken. Missing work had begun to draw attention from supervisors, which only deepened her sense that the life she had built was collapsing.

By the time she sought help, Moana was frightened by how small and barren her world had become. She was not coming with much hope in recovery; hope itself felt like something she had lost. But she was afraid that if nothing changed, she would lose her job, damage her marriage, and remain trapped with those few unbearable pictures and sounds of her brother’s death as the only parts of him her mind would allow her to keep.
